analysis.one_liner: Expands federal workplace anti-discrimination and harassment protections and phases out the sub-minimum wage for tipped workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced on February 13, 2026 with 23 Democratic cosponsors and referred to five House committees, the bill has seen no further action as Congress remains in session.
analysis.plain_summary: The BE HEARD in the Workplace Act would overhaul federal employment civil rights law. It would require employers with 15 or more workers to adopt and enforce anti-harassment policies and training, apply anti-discrimination protections to employers with just one employee, codify that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is sex discrimination, remove caps on compensatory and punitive damages, extend the time workers have to sue, bring independent contractors, interns, and volunteers under the law, bar employers from forcing workers into private arbitration over discrimination claims, and restrict nondisclosure agreements. It would also raise the special minimum wage for tipped workers in annual steps until it equals the full federal minimum wage, which is currently $2.13 an hour for workers whose tips are supposed to bring them up to the standard minimum.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face harassment or discrimination — especially women, LGBTQ workers, tipped restaurant workers, workers at very small employers, and contractors, interns, and volunteers who are currently outside the law — plus low-income workers who would get grants for free legal help.

how_it_helps.text: Phases out the $2.13 tipped minimum wage by raising it in annual steps until tipped workers earn the full federal minimum wage, and guarantees employees the right to keep their tips.
Makes sexual orientation, gender identity, sex stereotype, sex characteristics, and pregnancy discrimination explicitly unlawful forms of sex discrimination under Title VII and related laws.
Extends anti-discrimination protections to employers with as few as one employee (down from 15) and to independent contractors, interns, fellows, volunteers, and trainees.

Removes statutory caps on compensatory and punitive damages in discrimination cases and lets a single incident of harassment qualify, with incidents judged in the totality of the circumstances rather than under a strict severity threshold.
Extends the statutes of limitations for filing discrimination claims and the deadlines for federal employees to file complaints.
Prohibits employers from requiring workers to arbitrate discrimination claims, protects concerted legal action, and restricts nondisclosure agreements covering discrimination.

Requires employers with 15 or more employees to maintain, post, and disseminate comprehensive nondiscrimination policies, with fines of up to $1,000 per violation ($5,000 for repeat or willful violations), and directs the EEOC to set interactive training requirements.

Funds a national prevalence survey on workplace harassment, studies of harassment in the federal government and in enforcement, and grants for legal assistance for low-income workers and state advocacy systems.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — large and small — who would bear compliance costs for policies and training, face uncapped damages and longer filing windows in lawsuits, lose the tipped-employee wage credit (especially full-service restaurants), and lose the ability to force discrimination claims into arbitration.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, especially restaurants and small firms

drawbacks.text: All employers with 15 or more workers would face new mandates to adopt, post, and periodically update nondiscrimination policies and to provide training, with per-offense fines of $1,000 or more for noncompliance — a real compliance cost, particularly for small and low-margin businesses.

The bill would apply anti-discrimination law to employers with a single employee and to contractors and volunteers, and would remove caps on compensatory and punitive damages while extending filing deadlines and easing the standard of proof — changes that meaningfully increase litigation exposure for employers, which critics of similar proposals have argued raises liability costs and defensive hiring practices.

Eliminating the tipped minimum wage would raise labor costs substantially for restaurants and other tipped-wage employers, who argue (based on how the tip credit works) that the increase flows into menu prices or reduced staffing; the bill phases the change in over multiple years but ultimately requires the full minimum wage in cash wages.

The bill would bar the Religious Freedom Restoration Act from providing a defense to Title VII claims, a provision that religious-liberty advocates object to on the ground that it narrows statutory religious exemptions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver substantial protections to millions of workers — particularly tipped workers earning $2.13 an hour in base pay and workers currently excluded from the law — at a real but ordinary cost to employers in compliance and litigation exposure. The harassment-prevention infrastructure (policies, training, grants, research) is uncontroversial in design; the contested parts are the expanded coverage, uncapped damages, arbitration ban, and tipped-wage phase-out. The tipped-wage change is phased in over several years, which softens the transition for employers but delays the benefit for workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to five House committees — Education and Workforce plus Judiciary, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Veterans' Affairs — and no committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced the BE HEARD in the Workplace Act on February 13, 2026, joined by 14 original cosponsors listed on the bill.

The same day, the Speaker's referral sent the bill to the Committee on Education and Workforce and, in addition, to the Committees on the Judiciary, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Veterans' Affairs, with jurisdiction divided by provision — a five-committee referral that requires multiple committees to act before the bill could reach the floor.
A total of 22 Democratic members had cosponsored the bill as of the latest cosponsor list, with no Republican cosponsors recorded.
The action history shows no hearings, markups, votes, or further referrals after the initial committee referral, and Congress remains in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has lost anything, because the bill has not advanced far enough to change anyone's obligations; employers and tipped-wage businesses are simply spared any new requirements because the bill sits untouched in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, for now — no new rules

for.name: Rep. Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 13, 2026 and assembled 14 original cosponsors.

for.name: 22 Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 23 total supporters in the House.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats and there are no recorded votes, so no member of the other party has yet supported the bill on the record; opposition so far takes the form of committees not acting.

industries.note: The bill phases out the tip credit, which currently lets these employers pay as little as $2.13 an hour in cash wages and count tips toward the minimum wage. Their current labor-cost advantage is the direct loss to tipped workers the bill corrects.

industries.industry: Employers that use mandatory arbitration agreements
industries.note: The bill would prohibit forcing workers to arbitrate discrimination claims and restrict related NDAs, removing a tool employers use to keep harassment and discrimination disputes out of court, where damages would also become uncapped.

Federal anti-discrimination law would newly apply to employers with one or more employees; the bill pairs this with EEOC-provided model policies and trainings designed for small businesses, which softens but does not eliminate the compliance burden.

industries.industry: Worker-side employment lawyers and legal aid organizations
industries.note: The bill authorizes grants for civil legal assistance for low-income workers and a state advocacy system, and the expanded coverage and uncapped damages widen the pool of viable claims these firms can take.

analysis.trajectory: With the bill sitting in five committees, no Republican cosponsors, and only about eleven months left in the 119th Congress, the realistic path is that it dies in committee at the end of this Congress — the same fate as earlier versions of this proposal — unless its provisions get attached to a larger must-pass bill.
